decks.title: The Forgiving Fortress
decks.objective: The slot that has to survive turns 1-5 against a fast start, then convert everything it accumulated into a decisive finish. This is the deck you learn combat math on, so it should punish very few mistakes and reward patience.
decks.archetype: Toughness-and-lifegain fortress — a defensive shell that survives long enough for an accumulation payoff to close the game.
decks.whatItIs: Every one of its five approaches leans on high-toughness bodies and steady lifegain to take the earliest hits without losing tempo, then converts whatever it stockpiled — counters, life, or a graveyard — into a finish once the table has spent its removal on someone else.
decks.fitAmongTen: This is the lineup's teaching slot. It punishes very few mistakes, so it is where combat math, blocking assignments, and "when do I actually need to hold up an answer" get learned without a harsh tax for getting them wrong.
decks.playstyle: Early turns are quiet: you develop toughness and let opponents trade removal on each other. Threat assessment shifts around turn 6-8 once the fortress plan is online, and games often end not with a single haymaker but a fortress that simply refuses to fall over.
decks.mood: Patient and low-variance — a deck to play when you want a game you can think your way through rather than one that swings on a single draw.

complexity.why: The core loop — block, gain life, keep threats alive — reads directly off the board with little hidden information to track.

decks.winCondition: Combat damage once the board stabilizes and the accumulated advantage (counters or a graveyard package, depending on variant) tips games that would otherwise stall out.
decks.asksOfYou: Patience above all — resisting the urge to race, and correctly reading when the table has run out of removal for your threats.
decks.whenToPickThis: Build this first if you are new to the pod or want a deck that keeps you in the game past the early turns while you learn everyone else's threats.

priorityRank.rationale: Lowest decision density and the most forgiving mistake tolerance of the ten — the natural first build.

decks.priorityNote: Reflects the full ten-deck lineup, spanning common and expert play styles across a shared non-capstone budget band (with the Capstone alone set higher by design).

decks.title: The Long Game
decks.objective: The high-ceiling slot — the deck you grow into over months. It should reward reading the table, answering only what genuinely needs answering, and out-lasting three opponents through accumulated advantage rather than a single explosive turn.
decks.archetype: Proliferate-and-control long game — grinds three opponents down with incremental advantage rather than racing anyone.
decks.whatItIs: The five approaches split between a proliferate/counters engine (planeswalkers and permanent counters) and a pure control shell built on repeated removal and card advantage. Both read the same way at the table: nothing dies to you quickly, and you are still doing something on turn 15.
decks.fitAmongTen: This is the deck built to reward reading the table over any single game plan. It has the least fixed shape of the ten — its identity depends heavily on which of the five commanders you build around — which makes it the slot for someone who wants to specialize rather than follow a template.
decks.playstyle: Slow starts, deliberately. You are not applying pressure in the first five turns; you are answering threats and accumulating small, permanent advantages that compound. The back half of the game is where this deck actually plays.
decks.mood: Controlled and cerebral — satisfying if you enjoy a deck that improves its position every single turn rather than one that needs "the turn."

complexity.why: Correct sequencing of counters and removal against three unknown opponents, and recognizing which threats are worth an answer, both take real reps to get right.

decks.winCondition: Whatever the table has left after its resources are exhausted — usually a planeswalker ultimate, an oversized threat that finally resolves, or simple attrition once no one else has cards or answers left.
decks.asksOfYou: Judgment under uncertainty — knowing which of three opponents' threats to answer now versus which to let ride, with no reliable way to take that back once a removal spell is committed.
decks.whenToPickThis: Pick this once you already have a fortress or budget deck under your belt and want the slot that rewards paying attention to the whole table, not just your own hand.

priorityRank.rationale: Among the more demanding non-capstone decks for decision complexity, and its flagship build carries real budget risk from a single shell card whose market price can spike well past the rest of the list — best tackled once you're comfortable evaluating a purchase against a moving price.

decks.priorityNote: Reflects the full ten-deck lineup, spanning common and expert play styles across a shared non-capstone budget band (with the Capstone alone set higher by design).

decks.title: The Snowball
decks.objective: The compounding slot — a commander that fires for free every time another permanent lands, so each turn's play makes the next one bigger. It should feel like no turn is wasted, reward patience with returns that stack, and eventually produce an overwhelming position rather than a sudden kill.
decks.archetype: Permanent-drop engine — a commander whose trigger reads "whenever another permanent you control enters," played behind as many cheap permanents per turn as the deck can find. Three of its five approaches feed that engine with lands, one with enchantments, one with creature tokens.
decks.whatItIs: All five put a free repeating trigger on the table and then spend the game maximizing how often it fires, so the board looks meaningfully bigger on turn 10 than in decks that are still assembling a plan. What the trigger pays is the difference — Aesi, Sythis and the Gitrog Monster turn each drop into cards, Omnath into 5/5 bodies, Purphoros into damage aimed straight at the table.
decks.fitAmongTen: Where deck 1 survives and deck 2 answers, this deck simply accumulates — its progress is visible on the board every turn rather than gated behind a combo piece or a stabilized board state, which makes it easy to track your own position at a glance.
decks.playstyle: Every permanent you play does something the moment it lands, often literally triggering the commander. There is no dead turn 3 — even a "do nothing" turn advances the plan — and the back half of the game is spent converting a lead in permanents into a hand full of cards, a board full of bodies, or a life total the table cannot recover.
decks.mood: Steady and satisfying — for players who like watching a number (permanents, mana, board presence) climb turn over turn rather than waiting for one big swing.

complexity.why: The core loop rewards playing your cheapest permanent and passing; there's little bluffing or hidden-information reasoning required to execute the plan correctly.

decks.winCondition: An overwhelming lead in permanents, cashed out differently by build — a ramp-fueled string of oversized threats, a board of tokens, or on the burn variant, direct damage that scales with how many creatures you've played.
decks.asksOfYou: Consistency more than cleverness — sequencing your drops so the trigger fires as often as possible and not skipping a turn's development, since the whole plan is additive.
decks.whenToPickThis: A strong second or third build: nearly as forgiving as the fortress deck, but it starts teaching you to think about board state and long-term resource advantage instead of just combat math.

priorityRank.rationale: Nearly as low-complexity as the fortress deck, with the added benefit of teaching resource-advantage thinking that the more advanced decks in the lineup depend on.

decks.priorityNote: Reflects the full ten-deck lineup, spanning common and expert play styles across a shared non-capstone budget band (with the Capstone alone set higher by design).

decks.title: The Reactive Engine
decks.objective: The slot that reads three opponents and responds intelligently. It should hold the fort with cheap answers, accrue value passively while doing so, and eventually reach a position where the accumulated engine simply wins.
decks.archetype: Reactive value engine — cheap answers plus a passive value stream that eventually just wins on its own.
decks.whatItIs: Across its five approaches this deck holds the fort with efficient removal or defensive bodies while a passive engine (card draw off defenders, blink value, or an artifact toolbox) accrues advantage in the background, so you are never spending a turn doing nothing.
decks.fitAmongTen: This is the lineup's cheapest, most budget-forgiving slot, and it reads three opponents rather than following a fixed script, which makes it the natural pairing to the more linear decks elsewhere in the ten.
decks.playstyle: You are almost always holding up an answer rather than tapping out, and the engine ticks along on its own during opponents' turns. Games often look uneventful from your side until the accumulated card advantage from a dozen small triggers suddenly puts you far ahead.
decks.mood: Calm and reactive — rewards patience and punishes an opponent's overextension rather than forcing your own action.

complexity.why: Knowing when to hold up interaction versus when to develop, and tracking a slow-building engine's value over many turns, takes more judgment than the fortress or infrastructure decks but less than the proliferate/control slot.

decks.winCondition: Accumulated card and board advantage from the passive engine, eventually cashed in on a wide alpha strike or a value lead too large for the table to fight through.
decks.asksOfYou: Discipline to hold up answers instead of developing your own board, and the memory to track a slow-accruing engine's state turn over turn.
decks.whenToPickThis: Pick this when budget is the binding constraint — it is the cheapest complete build in the lineup — or when you want a deck that plays well reactively against decks you don't control.

priorityRank.rationale: The lineup's lowest all-in cost makes it an easy early acquisition even though its reactive decision-making is a step up from the fortress and infrastructure decks.

decks.priorityNote: Reflects the full ten-deck lineup, spanning common and expert play styles across a shared non-capstone budget band (with the Capstone alone set higher by design).

decks.title: The Immediate Engine
decks.objective: The fast-rhythm slot — something happens every turn from turn four onward. It should be the deck you reach for when you want action rather than patience, while still surviving a wipe.
decks.archetype: Fast, always-doing-something midrange — five different engines (spells-matter, voltron, tokens, graveyard, tribal) that all share one trait: constant turn-by-turn action starting around turn four.
decks.whatItIs: Where the other decks in the lineup ramp up slowly, this one is built to have a relevant play every turn from the early game on — casting spells that trigger a payoff, equipping and attacking, or building a token board — so there's rarely a pass-with-nothing-happening turn.
decks.fitAmongTen: This is the tempo counterweight to the patient decks elsewhere in the ten: where the fortress and infrastructure decks reward waiting, this one rewards constant small actions, which makes it the pick when you want a game that feels busy rather than measured.
decks.playstyle: Turns come with a decision almost every time — cast the spell that triggers the commander, attack with an equipped threat, or add to a growing token board — and the deck still carries enough resilience to take a board wipe and keep functioning.
decks.mood: Energetic and hands-on — for a session where you want to be doing something every turn rather than assembling a long-game plan.

complexity.why: Sequencing spells or attacks for maximum trigger value takes practice, though the payoff — more cards, more damage, more tokens — is usually immediate and legible.

decks.winCondition: Accumulated small triggers — extra cards, extra damage, extra bodies — compounding into a lethal turn faster than the slower decks in the lineup can set up their own finish.
decks.asksOfYou: Tempo awareness: sequencing plays to maximize triggers per turn, and recognizing when to convert accumulated value into an attack rather than continuing to build.
decks.whenToPickThis: Pick this when you want a deck that feels active from turn one rather than one you have to wait out — good variety alongside the fortress or infrastructure deck if you want your games to play differently from each other.

priorityRank.rationale: Comes in print and cheap — its precon-based build already clears the lineup's budget with room to spare — but the trigger-sequencing it rewards is a genuine step up from the lineup's beginner-tier decks.

decks.priorityNote: Reflects the full ten-deck lineup, spanning common and expert play styles across a shared non-capstone budget band (with the Capstone alone set higher by design).

decks.title: The Capstone
decks.objective: The flagship — the deck that out-resources three opponents and can win from behind. It should reward the most decisions per turn and be the one you graduate into once the other nine feel automatic.
decks.archetype: The flagship — graveyard-value, reanimation, ramp, and ETB-doubling engines that all resource out the table from behind, at a price point the other nine decks don't carry.
decks.whatItIs: Every approach here squeezes double value from the same cards — recurring them from the graveyard, doubling their enter-the-battlefield triggers, or ramping into a mana advantage so large that card disadvantage stops mattering. It is built to keep functioning after the kind of setback — a wipe, a key piece removed — that would end one of the other nine decks' games.
decks.fitAmongTen: This is deliberately one of the most demanding slots, and the most expensive, in the lineup, sitting outside the budget band the other nine decks share. It exists to be the one you build last, once the fundamentals — combat math, resource tracking, table reading — are second nature from the other nine.
decks.playstyle: Every card is doing at least one and a half jobs: a creature that returns from the graveyard, an ETB that fires twice, a land drop that ramps into the next threat. Games are won from behind more often than from ahead, since the resource engine keeps generating value even after a setback that would sink a simpler deck.
decks.mood: Ambitious and resilient — for a session where you want maximum decisions per turn and a plan that survives disruption rather than one that needs a clean start.

complexity.why: Tracking recursion targets, ETB triggers, and mana efficiency simultaneously, across a much higher card and combo density than the other nine decks, is genuinely demanding to play well.

decks.winCondition: An overwhelming resource and board advantage rebuilt turn after turn until no remaining opponent can keep pace, typically closed out by whichever finisher the accumulated value most directly enables — reanimated threats, doubled triggers, or a ramp-fueled bomb.
decks.asksOfYou: Full attention — tracking what's in every graveyard, what triggers twice, and sequencing plays to maximize value extracted per card, with a real cost for getting the order wrong.
decks.whenToPickThis: Build this last, once the other nine decks feel automatic to pilot — that's not just a suggestion, it's the deck's own design intent, and its higher, separate budget band reflects that it's meant to be a destination rather than a starting point.

priorityRank.rationale: By design and by its own higher budget band, this is the graduation deck — build it once the other nine are comfortable.

decks.priorityNote: Reflects the full ten-deck lineup, spanning common and expert play styles across a shared non-capstone budget band (with the Capstone alone set higher by design).

decks.title: The Combat Clock
decks.objective: The aggression slot — put a threat on the board that grows every turn and force the table to answer it in combat, while staying resilient enough that losing one creature doesn't lose you the game.
decks.archetype: Growing combat threat — equipment and counters piled onto one efficient body for four of its five approaches, and an evasive double-striker that grows the whole board for the fifth. Every build turns the attack step into a math problem the table has to solve exactly right.
decks.whatItIs: Four of its five approaches center combat math on one carefully protected creature, layering equipment and combat tricks until a couple of swings end the game — one grows its wearer for free on its own triggers, one goes wide with cheap equipment-tribal bodies as backup threats, one leans on raw size instead of counters, one turns exalted-style solo attacks into a blowout. The fifth spreads the growth instead of stacking it: a flying double-striker that hands out +1/+1 counters and evasive tokens at the beginning of every combat. All five convert "stick a threat, keep it alive" into a fast clock.
decks.fitAmongTen: Deck 5 already offers a Voltron-flavored commander among its five alternatives, but only as one of five different strategic identities sharing that slot. This is the lineup's deck fully committed to winning through the attack step — equipment on one creature as the default route, with one build that gets there by going wide in the air instead.
decks.playstyle: Early turns assemble mana and cheap threats; the moment your key creature is carrying two or three pieces — or the whole board has picked up counters — every combat becomes a math problem the table has to solve exactly right or lose. Exactly how the damage gets through — first strike, sheer size, flying, or simply out-racing the table — depends on which of the five you're playing.
decks.mood: Direct and confrontational — for a session where you want a visible, escalating threat and the tension of protecting whatever is carrying your game plan.

complexity.why: The game plan reads directly off the board — grow it, attack, win — with the one real skill being timing: don't over-commit into an open board wipe or a removal spell you should have played around.

decks.winCondition: Commander damage or raw combat damage, usually inside a handful of turns once the threat starts sticking — from one massively equipped creature on four of the builds, and from a board of flying tokens carrying counters on the fifth.
decks.asksOfYou: Restraint as much as aggression — recognizing when the table has an answer up and holding a turn back, since this plan's biggest risk is losing everything to a single removal spell or wipe.
decks.whenToPickThis: Build this alongside the Fortress deck if you want two very different beginner-friendly games — one that wins by refusing to die, one that wins by making a threat the table can't afford to let live.

priorityRank.rationale: As approachable as the Fortress deck with an even more linear game plan, though concentrating on one growing threat carries more risk to a well-timed wipe.

decks.priorityNote: Reflects the full ten-deck lineup, spanning common and expert play styles across a shared non-capstone budget band (with the Capstone alone set higher by design).

decks.title: The Long Memory
decks.objective: The tribal value-engine slot — build toward "Storied" (three or more artifacts, legendaries, and/or Sagas) so Balin's discard-and-draw becomes a repeatable card-advantage-into-damage engine instead of a one-time refill.
decks.archetype: Mono-red-leaning Dwarf tribal — a wide, aggressive board of cheap Dwarves and red value creatures, backed by a commander that turns that density into card advantage, burn, or +1/+1 counters.
decks.whatItIs: Every one of its five approaches runs a real density of Dwarves and cheap red aggression, curving into the table before it can stabilize. Where they differ is what converts that board into a win — one refills your hand and burns opponents off legendary-and-artifact density, one doubles down on vehicles and crewing, one grows the whole team with counters, one turns every point of damage the deck deals into more damage, one reanimates the aggression that already traded away — but all five are built to close games fast on a wide, disposable board.
decks.fitAmongTen: The lineup's other value-engine decks (Snowball, Long Game, Capstone) all measure value in cards or board state. This is the only one that converts spent cards directly into opponents' life totals once its own built-in threshold is met, and the only mono-color deck in the ten — no color-fixing considerations at all, at the cost of a narrower card pool to draw from.
decks.playstyle: Early turns fill the board with cheap Dwarves almost as a side effect of just playing your hand. Once the deck's own payoff turns on, every subsequent attack or trigger compounds — exactly how depends on which of the five you're playing, from card-and-damage wheels to counters that snowball to burn that scales with the board.
decks.mood: Patient but punishing — a slow build toward a single flag flipping, after which the deck plays noticeably meaner than it did the turns before.

complexity.why: You're tracking a real game-state condition (are you Storied yet?) alongside the usual creature count and mana curve, and choosing when to trigger a full hand discard needs the refill to actually be worth it.

decks.winCondition: Incremental burn from repeated Storied-fueled discard-and-draw triggers, closed out by direct damage once the table's life totals are already ground down, or by whatever threats the refilled hand keeps deploying.
decks.asksOfYou: Discipline about the discard — dumping your whole hand for Balin's trigger is only good once Storied is live and the refill is worth more than what you gave up, so knowing when NOT to trigger it matters as much as knowing when to.
decks.whenToPickThis: Pick this once you're comfortable tracking one extra piece of game state beyond your own board — a natural second deck after the Fortress or Voltron decks, and a gentler mono-color entry point than the lineup's multicolor value engines.

priorityRank.rationale: The Storied condition and the discard-timing judgment it rewards put this a clear step above the lineup's beginner decks, though it's still more forgiving than the spell-sequencing or resource-denial decks that follow it.

decks.priorityNote: Reflects the full ten-deck lineup, spanning common and expert play styles across a shared non-capstone budget band (with the Capstone alone set higher by design).

decks.title: The Live Wire
decks.objective: The spellslinger slot — cast enough noncreature spells, and enough expensive ones, that Shantotto herself becomes the win condition: a growing, evasive-enough threat that also refuels your hand every time a big spell resolves.
decks.archetype: Izzet-leaning spellslinger — a critical mass of cheap instants and sorceries that the commander converts into card advantage, extra damage, or both, so every turn's spells are doing double duty.
decks.whatItIs: Every one of its five approaches runs a real density of cheap interaction and card selection to keep spells flowing, plus a top end of a few genuinely expensive spells built to maximize whatever the commander rewards. Where they differ is the exact payoff — one turns mana spent on spells directly into damage and cards off its own attack trigger, one doubles every magecraft trigger, one taxes opponents' spells while rewarding your own, one wins off sheer devotion and card advantage at the top of the curve, one recasts spells straight from the graveyard — but all five are built around casting as much, and as profitably, as the turn allows.
decks.fitAmongTen: Deck 5 offers a spells-matter commander as one of five different identities sharing that slot; this is the lineup's only deck built entirely around spell mana value as its core resource, rather than card count or board state, and the only one where the commander's own body is a direct byproduct of how the rest of the deck is played rather than a separate piece to develop.
decks.playstyle: Early turns are about density — casting anything to keep the curve moving and the commander's payoff live. The turn everything comes together, spending big on the right spell can end a game outright or refill your hand for the next one; exactly how depends on which of the five you're playing.
decks.mood: Kinetic and a little greedy — for a session where you want every turn to be a small optimization puzzle about how much mana you can spend and what it earns you.

complexity.why: Sequencing which spells to cast and when, protecting a commander with no evasion of her own until she's grown, and correctly valuing a turn that spends everything against a turn that holds up interaction, all take real practice.

decks.winCondition: Commander damage from a Shantotto grown well past lethal in a single big turn, or simple attrition from the card advantage her four-mana-plus triggers generate over a longer game.
decks.asksOfYou: Mana-efficiency judgment — knowing when spending everything for maximum Shantotto growth is correct and when it leaves you open, since unlike a creature-based threat she has no board presence at all until you've actually cast something.
decks.whenToPickThis: Pick this once you're comfortable with the lineup's simpler decks and want one that rewards planning a whole turn's mana in advance rather than making one decision at a time.

priorityRank.rationale: The spell-sequencing and commander-protection judgment this deck rewards put it ahead of the lineup's tribal and engine decks, on par with the Long Game's own reading-the-table demands.

decks.priorityNote: Reflects the full ten-deck lineup, spanning common and expert play styles across a shared non-capstone budget band (with the Capstone alone set higher by design).

decks.title: The Long Con
decks.objective: The resource-denial slot — the lineup's one deck that wins by making the game harder for everyone else to play rather than by building the biggest board or the fastest clock, using Grand Arbiter's own asymmetric tax to make every one of your spells cheaper exactly when theirs get more expensive.
decks.archetype: Tax-and-control stax — resource denial or asymmetric taxation that slows the whole table down, backed by enough card draw and interaction to survive being everyone's obvious first target.
decks.whatItIs: Every approach runs a real density of taxation, selective denial, removal, and card draw to both survive the resulting slower games and convert the advantage into a win. Where they differ is the exact lever — one taxes spells asymmetrically in your favor, one taps down permanents and steals extra combats, one tutors for and abuses a scary enchantment suite, one strips resources outright through edicts and sacrifice, one steals and casts the table's own cards — but all five are built to make sure the game goes long enough for that edge to matter.
decks.fitAmongTen: This is the only deck in the ten whose entire plan is making other players' games worse rather than making your own better — every other deck wins by outracing, out-lasting, or out-resourcing the table; this one wins by making the table unable to function at all. It shares the lineup's standard budget band but is a completely different kind of deck to sit across from.
decks.playstyle: Early turns deploy taxes and interaction rather than threats, deliberately slowing the whole game down while you develop under an edge your opponents don't get. Wins arrive late, and often look less like a single big turn than a table that simply can't do anything anymore; exactly which lever gets there depends on which of the five you're playing.
decks.mood: Controlled and a little confrontational — genuinely satisfying if you enjoy denial and long-game planning, but this is the deck most likely to draw table attention early, and it asks you to be comfortable with that.

complexity.why: Timing taxation so it slows the table more than it slows you, tracking which of three opponents' resources are actually being denied, and managing the social dynamic of being the deck everyone wants to remove first, is a different and harder kind of demanding than any other deck in the lineup.

decks.winCondition: Whatever the table has left once its resources are taxed into paralysis — typically a slow attrition win or a single finisher that resolves because no one else can interact with it anymore.
decks.asksOfYou: Social and tactical patience in equal measure — correctly judging how much to tax the table before it becomes a bigger target than the game can bear, and playing a genuinely different, slower game than everyone else at the table.
decks.whenToPickThis: Build this only once you're comfortable with every other deck in the lineup and specifically want the lineup's one true expert-level, socially demanding archetype — this is the deck the "expert play style" brief was written for.

priorityRank.rationale: The social and tactical demands of resource denial make this the hardest deck in the lineup to pilot well, edged out of last place only by the Capstone's own higher, separate budget band and its role as the lineup's explicit graduation deck.

Modeled odds that a given opponent has not met this commander and build before. Input is the commander's live EDHREC play rank (5407 of ~30,000 tracked cards) on a log familiarity curve, bumped up if it is a precon face commander, then reduced by how far this upgrade package moves the deck off any list someone might already recognize.

Precon seed

Squirreled Away Bloomburrow 2024 In print ~$30 $55 total
Why this commander

A one-card loop. Saprolings die, every opponent loses life, you gain it, and you can pay to kill your own tokens whenever you like. A board wipe stops being a disaster and becomes a stack of drain triggers.

Key upgrades

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Blood Artist{1}{B}Creature — VampireAny creature dying drains each opponent. The keystone.$3.09
Zulaport Cutthroat{1}{B}Creature — Human RogueRedundant copy of the drain effect.$1.41
Bastion of Remembrance{3}{B}EnchantmentThird copy, on an enchantment that survives creature wipes.$0.28
Poison-Tip Archer{3}{B}{G}Creature — Elf ArcherFourth drain, plus deathtouch/reach that eats Dragons and Dinos.$1.54
Deadly Dispute{1}{B}InstantSac a token in response to removal: draw 2 and make a Treasure.$0.26
Tendershoot Dryad{4}{G}Creature — DryadA Saproling every upkeep — yours AND theirs — that grows the whole tribe. The city-builder this list was missing.$1.04
Fungal Plots{1}{G}EnchantmentGraveyard creatures become Saprolings; spare Saprolings become cards. Quiet, engine-shaped value.$0.25
Dictate of Erebos{3}{B}{B}EnchantmentYour creature dies, everyone sacrifices. Beats big-creature decks. Stretch.$16.60

How it plays

You never need to attack. Fodder plus a sacrifice outlet plus a drain enchantment are three unrelated cards that together end the game — genuinely convergent. The catch against your profile: it has no real early defense, so a rush deck can pressure you before the pieces assemble.

  • Friendly: mixed. Nobody loses their stuff, but slow table-wide drain can feel oppressive.
  • Fortress: the weak point. You block by trading, not by walling.

Room to grow — what this framework supports later

Upgrade value~$11 ea

The two dot rows score 35 cards costing about $401 in total — roughly $11 a card, or 8.7 upgrades per $100. That total is the 8 upgrades listed above, plus about 24 more archetype-specific cards on the advanced ladder (~$210), plus the 3 Game Changers below (~$113). Headroom is how long that whole ladder is; Upgrade value is how cheaply it climbs.

The next cards you would buy

Where it sits on the Bracket 2 – 3 line

Bracket 2
Core2.63Bracket 3

Upper Bracket 2 · 0 of 3 Game Changers used

Bracket 2 (“Core”) allows no Game Changers and no two-card infinite combos, and expects games to be satisfying from turn 8. Bracket 3 (“Upgraded”) allows up to three Game Changers, with combos only as a late finish, and expects games from turn 6. Tutor limits were removed from Brackets 1–3 in the October 2025 revision, so tutors do not move this number. The position above is scored from effect-per-mana, clock, interaction density, card advantage, resilience, the modeled turn-8 assembly odds and total spend.

Game Changers in this build
  • None — this build is Game-Changer-free, which is what keeps it inside Bracket 2.
The Maxed rung — 3 color-legal Game Changers, about $113
Game Changer$What it replaces, and what it buys you
Crop Rotation$4Takes the ramp slot held by Sol Ring. Search your library for a land card, put that card onto the battlefield, then shuffle.
Demonic Tutor$62Takes the tutor slot held by Corpse Connoisseur. Search your library for a card, put that card into your hand, then shuffle.
Orcish Bowmasters$47Takes the removal slot held by Origin of Metalbending. When this creature enters and whenever an opponent draws a card except the first one they draw in each of their draw steps, this creature deals 1 damage to any target.

Three is the ceiling: a fourth would put the deck in Bracket 4. These are not a shortlist — they are the cards the Maxed hundred runs. Each was tried in several slots in the list it would join, kept only where the deck did not measurably get worse over 3,000 simulated games, and confirmed afterwards on a seed the selection never saw. Prices are Scryfall market values.

Assembly is computed, not judged: hypergeometric odds across a 99-card library that the engine's required pieces are in hand or in play by turn 8 (7 opening cards + 8 draws + this deck's own draw output), then reduced by a disruption haircut for normal opponent removal. Commander-driven engines count the command zone as always available. The other five axes are scored against how the card actually performs in this shell, not in the abstract.

Honest caveat: Structurally the most resilient of the Deck 1 options, but the least aligned with 'strong defensive posture early'.
Claude’s 5th Place

Still fifth, but no longer for lack of a city: Tendershoot Dryad and Fungal Plots now give the swarm a genuine build-up engine, and Build-up moves to 5. What keeps it last in this row is unchanged and unfixable with cards — no walls, value measured in deaths, and a sacrifice identity the slot was deliberately steering away from.

Trey's Build · Deck 1
Fifth of five in this row

Big-Butt Defenders — Betor

Commander

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Betor, Ancestor's Voice{2}{W}{B}{G} Legendary Creature — Spirit DragonFifteen walls that normally cannot attack, plus three cards that let them hit for their toughness.$3.68

Deck rarity — by stage

Base83%Rarely seen
Tuned83%Rarely seen
Max86%Rarely seen

Modeled odds a given opponent has NOT met this commander and that stage of the build. The input is Betor, Ancestor's Voice's live EDHREC play rank — 5,347 of about 30,000 tracked cards — read on the same log familiarity curve the rest of this catalog uses, 10.51·ln(rank) − 7.1, which puts Base at 83%. Each rung above it is raised by how far that rung has moved off the recognizable list: (100 − previous) × changed/(changed + 16), with 0 cards changed at Tuned and 3 at Maxed.

Where the hundred comes from

Singles, not a box data/master-v2.json Owned and on order $6.40 of it already here $55.27 total

Base is that hundred with the Tuned pass undone, one displaced card restored per upgrade; Maxed is it with this deck's own Bracket-3 list applied. Every rung is exactly a hundred cards and no rung repeats a nonbasic.

Why this commander

You fill the board with 15 defenders that block anything, make mana (Overgrown Battlement, Axebane Guardian, Sylvan Caryatid, Wall of Roots) and replace themselves (Wall of Omens, Carven Caryatid). Assault Formation, Huatli, the Sun's Heart or Felothar the Steadfast then make every creature you control deal combat damage equal to its toughness, which turns a 0/13 into a 13-point attacker. Betor, Ancestor's Voice converts the deck's lifegain into +1/+1 counters at your end step and reanimates a creature whenever you lost life that turn.

How it wins

Tree of Perdition taps to swap an opponent's life total with its own 13 toughness, and one swing from Tree of Redemption with a toughness enabler out is exactly lethal from there. Otherwise you grind through with Indomitable Ancients, Canopy Gargantuan and Salvation Colossus, or fly over with Zetalpa, Primal Dawn and Dragonlord Dromoka.

Key cards

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Betor, Ancestor's Voice{2}{W}{B}{G}Legendary Creature — Spirit DragonTurns each turn's lifegain into +1/+1 counters and reanimates a creature whenever you also lost life.$3.68
Assault Formation{1}{G}EnchantmentTwo mana, makes the whole board deal damage equal to toughness, and can push a single defender in for {G}.$0.72
Felothar the Steadfast{1}{W}{B}{G}Legendary Creature — Human WarriorToughness damage plus the only effect that lets all your defenders attack, and a sacrifice outlet that draws.$3.05
Huatli, the Sun's Heart{2}{G/W}Legendary Planeswalker — HuatliA third copy of the toughness-damage effect, and its -3 gains life equal to your largest toughness, which feeds Betor.$0.46
Tree of Perdition{3}{B}Creature — PlantSets an opponent to 13 life from nowhere, which puts them in range of one attack.$2.94
Axebane Guardian{2}{G}Creature — Human DruidWith a full wall board it taps for four or five mana of any colors, powering out the eight-drops.$0.34
Salvation Colossus{6}{W}{W}Artifact Creature — ConstructA 9/9 that gives the whole team +2/+2 and indestructible on every attack, and comes back from the graveyard.$0.73

How it plays, turn by turn

Turns 1-3. Curve into mana walls: Wall of Roots or Overgrown Battlement on two, Axebane Guardian or Sylvan Caryatid on three. Wall of Omens and Carven Caryatid draw a card while they do it. Jaddi Offshoot and Grazing Gladehart start turning land drops into life.

Turns 4-6. Find a toughness enabler. Assault Formation on two is the cheapest, Huatli, the Sun's Heart on three, and Felothar the Steadfast on four also lets defenders attack at all. Betor on five then adds counters equal to your life gained each end step.

Turns 7+. Attack with 0/13s. Salvation Colossus makes the rest of the team +2/+2 and indestructible whenever you attack, Myr Battlesphere adds four bodies plus damage, and Sun Titan or Betor rebuilds after a wipe. Wall of Limbs sacrifices for a large chunk of life loss if you cannot get through.

Mulligan. Keep three or four lands with a green source plus a two- or three-mana mana wall (Wall of Roots, Overgrown Battlement, Axebane Guardian, Sylvan Caryatid) or Wall of Omens; with 39 lands you will draw more.

The four rungs, measured

Score is the engine's 0–100 composite, not a win percentage. ± is the standard error across the six seeds; two rungs differ meaningfully only when the gap is larger than twice the combined figure. Pod fun is the engine's own measure of whether the other three seats got a game.

The Pod Fun rung is the bench-only build: the optimiser was allowed to spend nothing and to search only cards already on Trey's shelf, with the win rate held under 60% as a hard constraint. It came back at 58.5%.

  • Fortress: maximum. Fifteen defenders that block anything, and thirty-nine lands behind them.
  • Convergence: also maximum, and it is the same fact from the other side — the walls do nothing at all until one of Assault Formation, Huatli or Felothar turns toughness into damage.
  • Friendly: you build a wall and wait. Nothing in the list takes anyone's things.

The six engine dots are read straight off the Tuned rung's measurement: average mana value for Rate, cards still stranded in hand at turn 8 for Card Adv., the average turn a won game ended for Clock, the share of turns 3–7 with an answer in hand for Interaction, mana screw plus flood for Resilience, and how often the commander actually landed for Assembly. The playstyle dots are a judgement, and the three lines above say which facts each one is standing on.

What to watch for

  • Only three cards turn toughness into damage - Assault Formation, Huatli, the Sun's Heart and Felothar the Steadfast. Draw none of them and 15 defenders just sit there.
  • 39 lands is the highest count of the six decks against an average mana value of 3.5, and only four cards are tagged card draw, so flooding is the most likely way you lose.
  • Betor's reanimate half only fires if you lost life that turn, and this deck gains life rather than losing it. Read the Bones, Painful Truths, Anguished Unmaking, Feed the Swarm and Sapling of Colfenor are the five cards that turn that half on.
  • Ritual of Soot, your own four-mana wipe, kills 17 of your 38 creatures. Wave of Reckoning and Fell the Mighty are the two wipes that spare a board of 0-power walls.

Room to grow — what this framework supports later

Headroom3 cards
Upgrade value~$15.75 ea

There are no Tuned swaps for this deck, so the 100 cards listed here are the Tuned build. All three Bracket-3 swaps are aimed at the failure modes above: Doran, the Siege Tower is a fourth toughness-damage effect so the plan survives removal, Guardian Project turns 38 creatures into a draw engine, and The Meathook Massacre adds a scalable wipe that drains while it clears.

  • Doran, the Siege Tower — $8.48

Game Changers in the Maxed hundred

The Maxed rung — 3 swaps, about $47.24
Card$What it replaces, and what it buys you
The Meathook Massacre$25.01Takes the slot Collective Effort holds. Scalable wipe that drains for every death - clears the pod's token engines while stacking Betor lifegain triggers. Marquee removal and win engine in one card.
Guardian Project$14.88Takes the slot Crashing Drawbridge holds. With 40+ creatures this draws on nearly every cast - converts the cheap wall curve into a card-advantage engine.
Doran, the Siege Tower$8.48Takes the slot Meandering Towershell holds. A second Betor effect in the 99 - every wall attacks and blocks with its toughness even when Betor is answered. Redundancy on the core mechanic is the #1 B3 fix.

The shape of the hundred

39 lands, 38 creatures, 7 instants, 10 sorceries, 3 artifacts, 1 enchantments, 2 planeswalkers. Average mana value 3.51. The roles it is built from: Removal 8, Finisher 5, Ramp 5, Protection 5, Lifegain 5, Toughness Payoff 4, Card Draw 4, Defender Ramp 4.

Could another legend in this deck lead it?

CommanderScoreWin rate

The hundred is identical in every row — only which of these cards starts in the command zone changes, and the other one plays in the ninety-nine. The field is the legends already inside this deck whose colour identity covers every card in it, not every legal commander in the colours, so this answers "is the right one already here?" and not "is there a better one anywhere?". Same engine, same table, same six seeds of 20,000 games.

Honest caveat: Only three cards turn toughness into damage. Draw none of them and fifteen defenders just sit there. Thirty-nine lands against an average mana value of 3.5 with four cards tagged card draw makes flooding the most likely way you lose — and Betor's reanimate half only fires on a turn you lost life, which this deck spends its time not doing.
Fifth of five in this row

The most one-sided deck of the six: it cannot lose the early game and cannot win without a specific card. All three Bracket-3 swaps are aimed exactly there — Doran is a fourth toughness-damage effect, Guardian Project turns thirty-eight creatures into a draw engine, and The Meathook Massacre is a wipe that drains while it clears.

Profile-tuned · Deck 1
Claude’s 3rd Place

Orzhov Lifegain Convergence — Liesa

Commander

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Liesa, Shroud of Dusk{2}{W}{W}{B} Legendary Creature — AngelFlying, lifelink. Each opponent loses 2 life whenever a creature they control dies... and your own spells cost life to recast from the yard.$0.88

Deck rarity — by stage

Base84%Rarely seen
Tuned88%Rarely seen
Maxed90%Rarely seen

Modeled odds that a given opponent has not met this commander and build before. Input is the commander's live EDHREC play rank (5589 of ~30,000 tracked cards) on a log familiarity curve, bumped up if it is a precon face commander, then reduced by how far this upgrade package moves the deck off any list someone might already recognize.

Precon seed

Any Orzhov lifegain box, or singles e.g. Wilds of Eldraine / Duskmourn shells Flexible seed ~$30 $80 total
Why this commander

Taxes every opponent's spell by two life and hands the life to you, passively, without ever targeting anyone. Next to lifelink blockers it turns your life total from a buffer into the deck's actual fuel.

Key upgrades

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Sanguine Bond{3}{B}{B}EnchantmentWhenever you gain life, target opponent loses that much.$5.98
Marauding Blight-Priest{2}{B}Creature — Vampire ClericA second Sanguine Bond on a body, for thirty cents. No loop, all redundancy.$0.30
Epicure of Blood{4}{B}Creature — VampireA third copy of the drain effect. The engine no longer lives on one enchantment.$0.31
Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose{2}{B}{B}Creature — Vampire ClericA creature-shaped Sanguine Bond — a second half to the combo.$10.74
Aetherflux Reservoir{4}ArtifactPay 50 life: deal 50 damage to any target. A third, independent convergence line.$20.12
Lyra Dawnbringer{3}{W}{W}Legendary Creature — Angel5/5 flying, first strike, lifelink; pumps your other Angels. Defense and clock in one.$0.46
Felidar Sovereign{4}{W}{W}Creature — Cat BeastAt upkeep, if you're at 40+ life, you win the game. A fourth win route.$1.96
Crested Sunmare{3}{W}{W}Creature — HorseAn indestructible 5/5 Horse every turn you gained life — a wipe-proof army.$8.89

How it plays

This is the deck your rant described. You spend the early game as the least attractive target at the table — lifelinking angels and horses, life total climbing, nobody profits from hitting you. Meanwhile you are quietly assembling four independent win routes: Sanguine Bond + Exquisite Blood, Vito + any lifegain, Aetherflux Reservoir, and Felidar Sovereign. Any two halves meeting ends the game across all three opponents simultaneously, and until that moment you look like the harmless lifegain player.

  • Convergence: the strongest in the entire lineup — four separate two-card kills, none obvious in isolation.
  • Fortress: lifelink plus high toughness plus a rising life total is the best anti-rush posture available.
  • Friendly: you take nothing from anyone; the kill is sudden and impersonal rather than a slow grind.

The two dot rows score 31 cards costing about $495 in total — roughly $16 a card, or 6.3 upgrades per $100. That total is the 8 upgrades listed above, plus about 20 more archetype-specific cards on the advanced ladder (~$300), plus the 3 Game Changers below (~$110). Headroom is how long that whole ladder is; Upgrade value is how cheaply it climbs.

Where it sits on the Bracket 2 – 3 line

Bracket 2
Core2.60Bracket 3
Upgraded
Upper Bracket 2 · 0 of 3 Game Changers used

Bracket 2 (“Core”) allows no Game Changers and no two-card infinite combos, and expects games to be satisfying from turn 8. Bracket 3 (“Upgraded”) allows up to three Game Changers, with combos only as a late finish, and expects games from turn 6. Tutor limits were removed from Brackets 1–3 in the October 2025 revision, so tutors do not move this number. The position above is scored from effect-per-mana, clock, interaction density, card advantage, resilience, the modeled turn-8 assembly odds and total spend.

Game Changers in this build
  • None — this build is Game-Changer-free, which is what keeps it inside Bracket 2.
The Maxed rung — 3 color-legal Game Changers, about $110
Game Changer$What it replaces, and what it buys you
Smothering Tithe$62Takes the ramp slot held by Mind Stone. Whenever an opponent draws a card, that player may pay {2}.
Orcish Bowmasters$47Takes the removal slot held by Protector of the Wastes. When this creature enters and whenever an opponent draws a card except the first one they draw in each of their draw steps, this creature deals 1 damage to any target.
Braids, Cabal Minion$1Takes the creature slot held by Danitha Capashen, Paragon. At the beginning of each player's upkeep, that player sacrifices an artifact, creature, or land of their choice.

Three is the ceiling: a fourth would put the deck in Bracket 4. These are not a shortlist — they are the cards the Maxed hundred runs. Each was tried in several slots in the list it would join, kept only where the deck did not measurably get worse over 3,000 simulated games, and confirmed afterwards on a seed the selection never saw. Prices are Scryfall market values.

Assembly is computed, not judged: hypergeometric odds across a 99-card library that the engine's required pieces are in hand or in play by turn 8 (7 opening cards + 8 draws + this deck's own draw output), then reduced by a disruption haircut for normal opponent removal. Commander-driven engines count the command zone as always available. The other five axes are scored against how the card actually performs in this shell, not in the abstract.

Honest caveat: Exquisite Blood is the expensive linchpin at $37. The deck still functions on Vito + Aetherflux + Felidar while you wait to find one.
Claude’s 3rd Place

Promoted to third by its own repair. Exquisite Blood is out of the Tuned list — it was a $37 linchpin AND, next to Sanguine Bond, an accidental two-card infinite in a Bracket 2 build. Blight-Priest and Epicure replace it: three cheap, loop-free copies of the drain effect, lifting assembly from 44% and dropping the price from $116 to inside the $40-110 brief. Exquisite waits on the ladder, clearly labelled as the combo piece.

Abzan Armor Tarkir: Dragonstorm 2025 In print ~$45 $79 total
Why this commander

The most flexible counter commander printed: creatures into counters, counters back into creatures, at instant speed, for free. That loop is the seed of half of Abzan's combos, which is why its upgrade ladder never runs out.

Key upgrades

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Ashnod's Altar{3}ArtifactSacrifice a creature for {C}{C}. With Ghave this becomes a loop that makes as many Saprolings as you have mana.$14.97
Blood Artist{1}{B}Creature — VampireTurns the loop into damage across all three opponents.$3.09
Cathars' Crusade{3}{W}{W}EnchantmentEvery token entering pumps the whole board — the go-wide payoff.$9.46
Mazirek, Kraul Death Priest{3}{B}{G}Legendary Creature — Insect ShamanEvery sacrifice grows the whole team.$0.35
Second Harvest{2}{G}{G}InstantDoubles your entire token board at instant speed.$5.14

How it plays

Ghave is a two-way converter, which is exactly the 'pieces that suddenly connect' shape. Early it just makes chump blockers and grows your board — completely unthreatening. Later, Ghave plus a free sacrifice outlet plus any drain effect is three unrelated cards that together end the game. It is the most engine-like Deck 1 option and it uses the box you were already buying.

variants.detailHtml:
Base Variant · Deck 1
Claude’s Choice

Ancestral Bulwark — Betor

Commander

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Betor, Ancestor's Voice{3}{W}{B}{G} Legendary Creature — Spirit DragonFlying, lifelink. At your end step, put +1/+1 counters on a creature equal to life gained this turn, and reanimate a creature with mana value ≤ life lost.$3.61

Deck rarity — by stage

Base65%Fairly familiar
Tuned69%Uncommon
Maxed73%Uncommon

Modeled odds that a given opponent has not met this commander and build before. Input is the commander's live EDHREC play rank (5396 of ~30,000 tracked cards) on a log familiarity curve, bumped up if it is a precon face commander, then reduced by how far this upgrade package moves the deck off any list someone might already recognize.

Precon seed

Abzan Armor Tarkir: Dragonstorm 2025 In print ~$45 $82 total
Why this commander

Two triggers in one end step, and they feed each other: life you gained becomes +1/+1 counters, life you lost reanimates a creature. Most commanders make you choose between growing and rebuilding. Betor does both off the same combat, without spending a card.

Key upgrades

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Soul Warden{W}Creature — Human ClericGain 1 life whenever any other creature enters — yours or theirs. Fires on everyone's turn, not just yours.$3.14
Authority of the Consuls{W}EnchantmentOpponents' creatures enter tapped AND you gain 1 life each. Blunts a rush and feeds Betor off the same card.$4.72
Pristine Talisman{3}ArtifactTaps for mana and gains 1 life. Guaranteed lifegain every single turn with zero setup — this is the card that makes the trigger reliable.$0.34
Trelasarra, Moon Dancer{G}{W}Legendary Creature — Elf ClericEvery lifegain event is a +1/+1 counter and a scry. A second Betor for two mana.$0.26
Dawn of Hope{1}{W}EnchantmentTurns lifegain into cards, and builds lifelink blockers with spare mana.$0.47
Blood Artist{1}{B}Creature — VampireDrains on every death anywhere — and it can target YOU: one death then feeds both halves of Betor at once.$3.09
Branching Evolution{2}{G}EnchantmentDoubles every +1/+1 counter you would place.$6.43
Well of Lost Dreams{4}ArtifactTurns your lifegain into cards.$0.99
Inspiring Call{2}{G}InstantDraw per counter-creature and make them indestructible — the only wipe answer.$0.20

How it plays

KEITH1Ramp behind walls, land Betor, then attack into damage on purpose so the lifegain converts to counters at end step. It runs almost on autopilot, which is exactly why it is forgiving — and exactly why it plateaus once you know the loop.

  • Fortress: best in the lineup — nothing attacks profitably into it.
  • Convergence: weak. Counters are additive, not combinatorial.
  • Wipes: one Inspiring Call is the entire insurance policy.

What Keith said

I don't see enough life gain in this deck to reliably trigger your commander. It's on a few creatures and your commander, and your commander can land a hit and trigger it, but having to attack with your commander is risky. I'd add more non-combat lifegain.
Good call — taken in full
  • Added six non-combat lifegain sources. Soul Warden, Authority of the Consuls, Pristine Talisman, Trelasarra, Dawn of Hope and Blood Artist. None of them require an attack, and three of them fire on opponents' turns.
  • Betor no longer has to swing. Pristine Talisman alone guarantees lifegain every turn just by tapping for mana, so the end-step trigger is live whether or not you go to combat.
  • Cut the counter redundancy that was doing nothing. Karn's Bastion, Contagion Clasp, Nesting Grounds, Evolution Sage and Conclave Mentor came out to pay for it — you had plenty of ways to multiply counters and almost no way to make the first one.
  • The road past Tuned leans into Betor's other half. The Maxed route now leads with Necropotence — paying life IS 'life lost this turn', which switches on the reanimation clause while refilling your hand — and Phyrexian Arena heads the ladder for the same reason.
  • Net cost +$7.27. $74.73 to $82.00.

Room to grow — what this framework supports later

Headroom34 cards
Upgrade value~$12 ea

The two dot rows score 34 cards costing about $411 in total — roughly $12 a card, or 8.3 upgrades per $100. That total is the 9 upgrades listed above, plus about 22 more archetype-specific cards on the advanced ladder (~$245), plus the 3 Game Changers below (~$137). Headroom is how long that whole ladder is; Upgrade value is how cheaply it climbs.

The next cards you would buy
  • Phyrexian Arena
  • The Ozolith
  • Innkeeper's Talent
  • Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider
  • Doubling Season

Where it sits on the Bracket 2 – 3 line

Bracket 2
Core2.57Bracket 3
Upgraded
High Bracket 2 · 0 of 3 Game Changers used

Bracket 2 (“Core”) allows no Game Changers and no two-card infinite combos, and expects games to be satisfying from turn 8. Bracket 3 (“Upgraded”) allows up to three Game Changers, with combos only as a late finish, and expects games from turn 6. Tutor limits were removed from Brackets 1–3 in the October 2025 revision, so tutors do not move this number. The position above is scored from effect-per-mana, clock, interaction density, card advantage, resilience, the modeled turn-8 assembly odds and total spend.

Game Changers in this build
  • None — this build is Game-Changer-free, which is what keeps it inside Bracket 2.
The Maxed rung — 3 color-legal Game Changers, about $137
Game Changer$What it replaces, and what it buys you
Aura Shards$28Takes the removal slot held by Damn. Whenever a creature you control enters, you may destroy target artifact or enchantment.
Smothering Tithe$62Takes the ramp slot held by The Mightstone and Weakstone. Whenever an opponent draws a card, that player may pay {2}.
Orcish Bowmasters$47Takes the removal slot held by Tree of Redemption. When this creature enters and whenever an opponent draws a card except the first one they draw in each of their draw steps, this creature deals 1 damage to any target.

Three is the ceiling: a fourth would put the deck in Bracket 4. These are not a shortlist — they are the cards the Maxed hundred runs. Each was tried in several slots in the list it would join, kept only where the deck did not measurably get worse over 3,000 simulated games, and confirmed afterwards on a seed the selection never saw. Prices are Scryfall market values.

Assembly is computed, not judged: hypergeometric odds across a 99-card library that the engine's required pieces are in hand or in play by turn 8 (7 opening cards + 8 draws + this deck's own draw output), then reduced by a disruption haircut for normal opponent removal. Commander-driven engines count the command zone as always available. The other five axes are scored against how the card actually performs in this shell, not in the abstract.

Honest caveat: Value lives on creatures as counters — the most wipe-fragile storage in Magic. Two removal spells in 100 cards cannot answer a growing threat across the table.
Claude’s Choice

The fixes changed this ranking. Before the lifegain rework this build could not reliably trigger its own commander; now six non-combat sources fire every turn, Blood Artist can point at you to switch on BOTH halves, and the Maxed route through Necropotence feeds the reanimation clause directly. It keeps the box and plan you already own, sits at $82 against a $110 brief, and scores 5/5 Fortress and Friendly. The best version of the deck you were already buying.

Trey's Build · Deck 2
Third of five in this row

Proliferate Counters — Atraxa

Commander

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Atraxa, Praetors' Voice{G}{W}{U}{B} Legendary Creature — Phyrexian Angel HorrorAtraxa proliferates at every end step, and sixteen other cards do it too, so every counter keeps growing.$29.43

Deck rarity — by stage

Base75%Uncommon
Tuned75%Uncommon
Max82%Rarely seen

Modeled odds a given opponent has NOT met this commander and that stage of the build. The input is Atraxa, Praetors' Voice's live EDHREC play rank — 2,475 of about 30,000 tracked cards — read on the same log familiarity curve the rest of this catalog uses, 10.51·ln(rank) − 7.1, which puts Base at 75%. Each rung above it is raised by how far that rung has moved off the recognizable list: (100 − previous) × changed/(changed + 16), with 0 cards changed at Tuned and 6 at Maxed.

Where the hundred comes from

Singles, not a box data/master-v2.json Owned and on order $57.27 of it already here $89.11 total

Base is that hundred with the Tuned pass undone, one displaced card restored per upgrade; Maxed is it with this deck's own Bracket-3 list applied. Every rung is exactly a hundred cards and no rung repeats a nonbasic.

Why this commander

You put counters on things cheaply - Merfolk Skydiver, Wall of Resurgence, Forgotten Ancient, Bristlebane Battler - and then grow them for free. Atraxa, Praetors' Voice proliferates at every one of your end steps, and 16 other cards proliferate as well, including Inexorable Tide, Flux Channeler, Evolution Sage, Thrummingbird, Grateful Apparition and Tekuthal, Inquiry Dominus. While that builds, 13 removal spells and four board wipes keep the rest of the table from running away with the game.

How it wins

Nothing in the deck costs more than five mana and there is no dedicated finisher, so you win by attacking with counter-inflated creatures behind Atraxa's 4/4 flying, vigilance, deathtouch, lifelink body. Viral Drake plus repeated proliferate is a real but slow second route, adding poison counters one at a time until an opponent hits ten.

Key cards

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Atraxa, Praetors' Voice{G}{W}{U}{B}Legendary Creature — Phyrexian Angel HorrorA free proliferate every end step on a 4/4 flying deathtouch lifelink body that also blocks everything.$29.43
Inexorable Tide{3}{U}{U}EnchantmentProliferate on every spell you cast, which is the deck's only true engine.$3.66
Deepglow Skate{4}{U}Creature — FishDoubles every counter on any number of permanents when it enters - the single biggest swing in the list.$0.28
Tekuthal, Inquiry Dominus{2}{U}{U}Legendary Creature — Phyrexian HorrorEvery proliferate becomes two, which doubles the output of all 16 proliferate cards.$1.47
Forgotten Ancient{3}{G}Creature — ElementalGrows on every spell anyone casts and hands its counters out to the rest of your board each upkeep.$0.33
Flux Channeler{2}{U}Creature — Human WizardThree mana, proliferates on every noncreature spell, and 32 of the 100 cards are noncreature, nonland spells.$3.49
Tragic Arrogance{3}{W}{W}SorceryYou choose what everyone keeps, so it is a wipe that leaves your best permanent standing.$0.25
Evolution Sage{2}{G}Creature — Elf DruidProliferates on every land drop, which makes even a flooded draw do work.$2.33

How it plays, turn by turn

Turns 1-3. Fix and ramp: Fertilid, Pilgrim's Eye, Axebane Guardian, Azorius Signet, Simic Signet, Everflowing Chalice, Wayward Swordtooth. Thrummingbird and Grateful Apparition on two both proliferate just by connecting for one damage, so play them into open boards.

Turns 4-6. Cast Atraxa on four if you have all four colors, then add a proliferate engine - Inexorable Tide, Flux Channeler or Evolution Sage - and start feeding Forgotten Ancient. Deepglow Skate doubles every counter on any number of permanents when it enters, which is often the biggest turn of the game.

Turns 7+. Tekuthal, Inquiry Dominus turns every proliferate into two. Hold up Go for the Throat, Anguished Unmaking, Mortify and Repel Calamity, and reset with Tragic Arrogance or Wave of Reckoning when someone gets ahead - Wave of Reckoning is safe for your low-power, counter-fattened creatures.

Mulligan. Keep three or four lands covering at least three of your four colors plus a two- or three-mana ramp piece; a hand that produces only two colors will not cast Atraxa on time.

The four rungs, measured

Every rung is the exact hundred this page publishes for it, played 120,000 times — six independent seeds of 20,000 games each — against the mixed pod in sim/opponents.json. Score is the engine's 0–100 composite, not a win percentage. ± is the standard error across the six seeds; two rungs differ meaningfully only when the gap is larger than twice the combined figure. Pod fun is the engine's own measure of whether the other three seats got a game.

The Pod Fun rung is the bench-only build: the optimiser was allowed to spend nothing and to search only cards already on Trey's shelf, with the win rate held under 60% as a hard constraint. It came back at 56.1%.

  • Build-up: Atraxa proliferates at every one of your end steps and sixteen other cards proliferate as well, so nothing you place ever stops growing.
  • Fortress: thirteen removal spells and four board wipes behind a 4/4 flying deathtouch lifelink blocker.
  • Longevity: the soft spot. Four creatures draw a card and there is no repeatable draw engine, so a wipe leaves you with nothing to rebuild from.

The six engine dots are read straight off the Tuned rung's measurement: average mana value for Rate, cards still stranded in hand at turn 8 for Card Adv., the average turn a won game ended for Clock, the share of turns 3–7 with an answer in hand for Interaction, mana screw plus flood for Resilience, and how often the commander actually landed for Assembly. The playstyle dots are a judgement, and the three lines above say which facts each one is standing on.

What to watch for

  • Card draw is close to nonexistent: only four creatures draw a card and there is no repeatable draw engine, so any board wipe leaves you with nothing.
  • The mana base is the real weakness - 27 of the 33 lands are basics, with only 9 white, 7 blue, 11 black and 7 green land sources, and Lotus Field sacrifices two lands when it enters.
  • Six creatures enter with -1/-1 counters they want to remove (Bristlebane Battler, Burdened Stoneback, Heirloom Auntie, Moonlit Lamenter, Reaping Willow, Reluctant Dounguard). Proliferate would add to those, so never point it at them.
  • The curve tops out at five with no finisher. If the game goes long you have to have removal in hand, because you cannot race anyone.

Room to grow — what this framework supports later

Headroom6 cards
Upgrade value~$12.85 ea

There are no Tuned swaps for this deck, so the 100 cards listed here are the Tuned build. The six Bracket-3 swaps attack both weak spots directly: Nature's Lore fixes the mana, Phyrexian Arena and Night's Whisper add the repeatable draw the list lacks, and Ichormoon Gauntlet, Pir, Imaginative Rascal and Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider make every counter you place count for more.

Game Changers in the Maxed hundred

The Maxed rung — 6 swaps, about $77.09
Card$What it replaces, and what it buys you
Phyrexian Arena$4.65Takes the slot Mirrodin Avenged holds. An extra card every upkeep - the raw, repeatable card advantage the current list lacks.
Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider$55.18Takes the slot Nightmare Sower holds. Marquee B3 payoff (NOT a Game Changer per Scryfall's official flag): doubles every counter you place and halves your opponents' - proliferate hits twice as hard while shutting down the pod's counter engines.
Ichormoon Gauntlet$4.80Takes the slot Rebellious Captives holds. Proliferate on every noncreature spell (30 in the deck), plus planeswalker modes Atraxa's end step compounds.
Pir, Imaginative Rascal$5.32Takes the slot Stony Strength holds. Every counter placed on your permanents gets +1 - quietly doubles proliferate output deck-wide.
Night's Whisper$5.42Takes the slot Troll Negotiations holds. Two cards for two mana; the life is paid back by Atraxa lifelink and Rhox Faithmender doubling.
Nature's Lore$2.69Takes the slot Origin of Metalbending holds. An untapped Forest at 2 mana - directly fixes the deck's biggest need: Atraxa reliably on turn 3-4.

The shape of the hundred

33 lands, 35 creatures, 11 instants, 5 sorceries, 8 artifacts, 8 enchantments. Average mana value 2.93. The roles it is built from: Proliferate 16, Removal 13, Counters Payoff 7, Ramp 5, Mana Rock 4, Board Wipe 4, Token Producer 2, Protection 2.

Honest caveat: Twenty-seven of the thirty-three lands are basics across four colours, and Lotus Field sacrifices two lands when it enters. Six creatures arrive with -1/-1 counters they want gone, so a careless proliferate makes them worse.
Third of five in this row

Four colours off a basic-heavy mana base, and the Bracket-3 list goes straight at both weak spots: Nature's Lore for the mana, Phyrexian Arena and Night's Whisper for the draw the deck does not otherwise have.

Profile-tuned · Deck 2
Claude’s Runner-up

Esper Pillowfort Longevity — Oloro

Commander

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Oloro, Ageless Ascetic{3}{W}{U}{B} Legendary Creature — Giant SoldierAt the beginning of your upkeep you gain 2 life — even while Oloro is in the command zone. Whenever you gain life, draw a card and each opponent loses 1.$19.92

Deck rarity — by stage

Base85%Rarely seen
Tuned88%Rarely seen
Maxed90%Almost never seen

Modeled odds that a given opponent has not met this commander and build before. Input is the commander's live EDHREC play rank (6337 of ~30,000 tracked cards) on a log familiarity curve, bumped up if it is a precon face commander, then reduced by how far this upgrade package moves the deck off any list someone might already recognize.

Precon seed

Any Esper shell + singles flexible Flexible seed ~$40 $91 total
Why this commander

Gains you life from the command zone whether you cast it or not. It is the only commander that pays you for doing nothing, which is exactly the subsidy a pillowfort deck needs while it sets up.

Key upgrades

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Ghostly Prison{2}{W}EnchantmentOpponents pay {2} per attacking creature. The fortress.$5.78
Propaganda{2}{U}EnchantmentThe second copy in blue — redundancy is what makes a pillowfort hold.$2.57
Approach of the Second Sun{6}{W}SorceryCast it twice and you simply win. The purest longevity win in Magic.$6.70
Test of Endurance{2}{W}{W}EnchantmentAt upkeep at 50+ life, you win.$8.52
Felidar Sovereign{4}{W}{W}Creature — Cat BeastAt upkeep at 40+ life, you win.$1.96
Sanguine Bond{3}{B}{B}EnchantmentConverts the passive lifegain into damage if you would rather close that way.$5.98

How it plays

This is the 'I was consistent and I was still there at the end' deck taken to its logical conclusion. Oloro pays you two life and a card every upkeep from the command zone, so you are ahead before you have played anything. Taxing enchantments make you the least efficient player to attack. You never sabotage anybody, you never swing, and somewhere around turn twelve you cast one spell twice and the game ends.

Bracket 2 (“Core”) allows no Game Changers and no two-card infinite combos, and expects games to be satisfying from turn 8. Bracket 3 (“Upgraded”) allows up to three Game Changers, with combos only as a late finish, and expects games from turn 6. Tutor limits were removed from Brackets 1–3 in the October 2025 revision, so tutors do not move this number. The position above is scored from effect-per-mana, clock, interaction density, card advantage, resilience, the modeled turn-8 assembly odds and total spend.

Game Changers in this build
  • None — this build is Game-Changer-free, which is what keeps it inside Bracket 2.
The Maxed rung — 3 color-legal Game Changers, about $107
Game Changer$What it replaces, and what it buys you
Thassa's Oracle$22Takes the finisher slot held by Mulldrifter. When this creature enters, look at the top X cards of your library, where X is your devotion to blue.
Rhystic Study$70Takes the draw slot held by Isperia, Supreme Judge. Whenever an opponent casts a spell, you may draw a card unless that player pays {1}.
Bolas's Citadel$15Takes the finisher slot held by Hypnotic Sprite // Mesmeric Glare. You may look at the top card of your library any time.

Three is the ceiling: a fourth would put the deck in Bracket 4. These are not a shortlist — they are the cards the Maxed hundred runs. Each was tried in several slots in the list it would join, kept only where the deck did not measurably get worse over 3,000 simulated games, and confirmed afterwards on a seed the selection never saw. Prices are Scryfall market values.

Assembly is computed, not judged: hypergeometric odds across a 99-card library that the engine's required pieces are in hand or in play by turn 8 (7 opening cards + 8 draws + this deck's own draw output), then reduced by a disruption haircut for normal opponent removal. Commander-driven engines count the command zone as always available. The other five axes are scored against how the card actually performs in this shell, not in the abstract.

Honest caveat: Two honest flags: Oloro is a Giant Soldier, the most humanlike commander in the matrix, and a pure pillowfort can read as unfun for opponents who want to attack something.
Claude’s Runner-up

The purest expression of your 'chess-like, still standing in the final two' line. Oloro pays you two life and a card every upkeep from the command zone, so you are ahead before you cast anything, and it wins without ever attacking. It scores 64% assembly and 5/5 on Longevity, Fortress and Friendly. Second because the clock is deliberately 1/5 — this deck cannot close, it can only outlast, and a hard pillowfort can read as unfun for opponents who came to attack something.

Base Variant · Deck 2
Claude’s 3rd Place

The Withering — The Reaper

Commander

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
The Reaper, King No More{2/B}{2/R}{2/G} Legendary Artifact Creature — ScarecrowETB: a -1/-1 counter on up to two creatures. Whenever an opponent's creature with a -1/-1 counter on it dies, you may put that card onto the battlefield under your control — once each turn. That is once each TURN, not each round: with deaths on other players' turns it can fire up to four times a rotation.$0.45

Deck rarity — by stage

Base66%Fairly familiar
Tuned70%Uncommon
Maxed74%Uncommon

Modeled odds that a given opponent has not met this commander and build before. Input is the commander's live EDHREC play rank (6085 of ~30,000 tracked cards) on a log familiarity curve, bumped up if it is a precon face commander, then reduced by how far this upgrade package moves the deck off any list someone might already recognize.

Precon seed

Blight Curse Lorwyn Eclipsed In print ~$28 $42 total
Why this commander

Turns removal into permanent shrinkage instead of a one-shot answer. -1/-1 counters stay put, so every small hit compounds across turns rather than resetting.

Key upgrades

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Necroskitter{1}{B}{B}Creature — ElementalA second Reaper with no once-per-turn clause: every opponent creature that dies holding a -1/-1 counter comes back under your control.$0.39
Hapatra, Vizier of Poisons{B}{G}Legendary Creature — Human ClericEvery -1/-1 counter you place also makes a 1/1 deathtouch Snake. Legal here because The Reaper is Jund, not Rakdos.$0.29
Kulrath Knight{3}{B/R}{B/R}Creature — Elemental KnightAnything holding a counter can't attack or block. The defensive piece the deck was missing.$0.23
Ichor Rats{1}{B}{B}Creature — Phyrexian RatThe card Keith called out. Infect: its damage IS -1/-1 counters, feeding every engine here.$2.06
Throne of Geth{1}ArtifactSacrifice an artifact: proliferate. The deck's one real sacrifice outlet.$1.02
Nest of Scarabs{2}{B}EnchantmentEvery -1/-1 counter also makes a 1/1 Insect.$3.99
Grim Affliction{2}{B}SorceryOne counter, then proliferate.$0.32
Serrated Arrows{4}ArtifactThree counters over three turns.$0.25

How it plays

Mark a threat, let it die, take it. The fantasy is excellent and the execution is a power tier short — your removal is sized for 2/2s in a pod full of 7/7s.

  • Friendly: low. Taking opponents' creatures is the highest-salt thing in the lineup.
  • Fortress: poor — you have no way to not-die while setting up.

What Keith said

Probably my favorite deck, this effect is so rare and stealing cards is a blast. Seems to be tons of synergy in the deck already. Ichor Rats is a great upgrade. Bloodbriar... are you sacrificing creatures? I don't think so...
Good call — taken in full
  • Bloodbriar is out. He was right — the only things this deck ever sacrifices are Throne of Geth eating an artifact and Nihil Spellbomb cashing itself in, so Bloodbriar was a vanilla 2/3 for three. Worse, it wants +1/+1 counters in a deck that deals exclusively in -1/-1 counters.
  • Necroskitter in its place. It is a second copy of the effect Keith likes, with no once-per-turn clause: any opponent creature that dies with a -1/-1 counter comes back under your control.
  • Blowfly Infestation was considered — and deliberately shelved. With Hapatra or Nest of Scarabs it is a true two-card infinite loop: a 1/1 token dies holding a counter, Blowfly re-places the counter, the replacement token dies, forever. Bracket 2 allows no two-card infinite combos, so Blowfly waits at the top of the advanced ladder as the Maxed-stage finisher, clearly labelled.
  • Hapatra and Kulrath Knight added. Hapatra turns each counter into a deathtouch Snake; Kulrath Knight stops anything holding a counter from attacking or blocking, which fixes the defensive hole.
  • Corrected the commander line. The Reaper costs {2/B}{2/R}{2/G} and its color identity is Jund, not Rakdos — the page had it wrong, which also means Golgari cards like Hapatra are legal here.
  • Net cost +$0.87. $41.20 to $42.07 — and Keith's Ichor Rats is now a headline card instead of a footnote.

Three is the ceiling: a fourth would put the deck in Bracket 4. These are not a shortlist — they are the cards the Maxed hundred runs. Claude’s 3rd Place

Keith's favourite, and the rework earned it a podium spot: Necroskitter and Hapatra now compound every counter with no infinite loop, Kulrath Knight closes the defensive hole, and Ichor Rats headlines. Third rather than higher for the same two honest reasons as before — Friendly 2, because taking creatures is still taking creatures, and the slowest clock in the row.

Input is the commander's live EDHREC play rank (835 of ~30,000 tracked cards) on a log familiarity curve, bumped up if it is a precon face commander, then reduced by how far this upgrade package moves the deck off any list someone might already recognize.

Precon seed

Any Simic ramp shell + singles flexible Flexible seed ~$40 $63 total
Why this commander

An extra land drop plus a card every time you play a land. It converts the single most reliable action in Magic into a repeatable draw engine with no setup at all.

Key upgrades

CardCostTypeWhat it does$
Tatyova, Benthic Druid{3}{G}{U}Legendary Creature — Merfolk DruidSecond copy of the draw-on-landfall effect, in the 99.$0.27
Kruphix, God of Horizons{3}{G}{U}Legendary Enchantment Creature — GodUnused mana carries over as colourless. Turns patience into a stockpile.$4.26
Wall of Blossoms{1}{G}Creature — Plant WallDefensive body that replaces itself.$0.26
Lotus Cobra{1}{G}Creature — SnakeLandfall: every land is a ritual. With Aesi's extra drop, two free mana a turn.$6.17
Rampaging Baloths{4}{G}{G}Creature — BeastLandfall: a 4/4 Beast per land — two a turn with Aesi. Inevitability with no splash required.$0.33
Growth Spiral{G}{U}InstantTwo mana at instant speed: a card and an extra land onto the battlefield. Aesi a turn early.$0.30
Explore{1}{G}SorcerySame effect at sorcery speed. Two copies of the accelerator the six-mana commander needed.$0.23

How it plays

Where Obuun converts lands into bodies, Aesi converts lands into cards — which is the more chess-like version of the same idea. You defend with cheap walls, bank mana with Kruphix, and every land drop refills your hand. The convergence turn is Kruphix unbanking a stockpiled mana pool into one enormous X-spell — or simply the fourth and fifth free Baloth hitting the table.

Three is the ceiling: a fourth would put the deck in Bracket 4. These are not a shortlist — they are the cards the Maxed hundred runs. Fourth, now with its one honest knock — a six-mana commander in a deck that did nothing to get there faster — directly patched: Growth Spiral and Explore put Aesi down a turn early while feeding the landfall engine. It stays behind 3o on trust: Keith signed the Obuun build, and this one's payoffs still arrive a turn later than Gitrog's or Sythis's.

The most under-the-radar deck here. You spend the game laying down harmless-looking enchantments and drawing cards off each one — no board presence to threaten anybody, nothing worth removing. Goblin Token Burn — Purphoros

Commander
